title: Pascal's wager
note: Pascal's wager is not an argument that God exists but that it is rational to wager on God when reason cannot settle the question. If God exists, the believer gains an infinite good; if not, little is lost. Objections: many possible gods, belief cannot be chosen at will, mixed strategies, and the ethics of believing for gain.

read.title: The wager
text: Pascal thought reason alone could not decide whether God exists: 'Reason can decide nothing here.' Yet we cannot simply stay neutral, since how we live is itself a bet. 'You must wager. It is not optional. You are embarked.' The argument, in its strongest form, runs:

(1) Either God exists or not, and reason cannot settle which. (2) You must in effect wager one way or the other. (3) Wagering for God has an infinite payoff if God exists and a finite cost if not. (4) Wagering against God has at best a finite payoff. (5) Any nonzero probability of an infinite payoff outweighs a finite cost. (6) So rationality requires wagering for God.
Pascal's own words: 'If you gain, you gain all; if you lose, you lose nothing. Wager, then, without hesitation that He is.'

The most famous objection is the many-gods objection, raised by Diderot: an imam could reason just as well this way. Many possible gods promise infinite rewards, so the wager seems to recommend everything at once, or nothing.

Defenders reply that the wager applies only among live options with some real evidence and tradition behind them. Not every invented deity has the same probability, and a god who rewards only unbelief is far less likely than the God of the great monotheistic traditions. Others add that the wager was meant for one who already doubts between Christianity and unbelief, not as a general proof.
